In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether dopamine encodes a prediction-error signal in the context of model-based reinforcement learning.
the question of whether the dopamine prediction-error signal reflects a single, scalar value, or multiple dimensions of the expected outcome.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
model-based predictions do influence dopamine, but the extent to which they do and what they influence is still an open question.

the dopamine system is not just involved in model-free reinforcement learning, but is also involved in model-based computations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
dopamine is a more complicated signal than we previously thought, but also more useful.
model-free and model-based learning are not mutually exclusive and that dopamine responses may reflect the interaction between both.
model-based and model-free learning are not separate, but rather complementary systems that interact with each other to produce adaptive learning and behavior.
The main takeaway from our work is that
dopamine is a complex signal, and that the phasic response is likely to be influenced by multiple computations.
the model-based computations underlying the phasic dopamine response are not well understood and are likely to be complex.
dopamine prediction errors are not simply the difference between an expected and received reward, but rather reflect a complex interaction between model-based and model-free learning processes.
